beats.trigger: ## Multi-Agent Systems
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Hire three agents to search. Three more to decide.
beats.got: Something about agents being hired like staff. That wording makes me nervous in a people context, and I'm not sure it's meant literally.

beats.trigger: [Schedule your personal agent](exercises/personal-agent-homework.md) to read your challenge memory for a week.
beats.got: Homework links I'd have to chase. I don't know what a challenge memory is yet.

beats.trigger: **Build** three source-finding agents, each in its source's dialect, and a helper-persona synthesizer
beats.got: Nothing I can use. 'Dialect' and 'helper-persona synthesizer' are used before anyone explains them. The word 'strategic' is the only part I understood.

beats.trigger: What do you expect will get lost between them?
beats.got: I'm being asked to guess what gets lost when agents hand work to each other. That's a fair question, and it sounds like handoffs between people.

beats.trigger: Writing a file changes your folder. Sending to Slack changes another system.
beats.got: An agent that acts in other systems gets a boundary and an approval step. That's a control I could explain to a works council. I wonder who approves in real life.

beats.trigger: Push back hard when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: I ask the agent to name the one thing blocking everything else. I like that it's about the decision I'd stay late to make. The pushing back is something I do anyway.

beats.trigger: Paste each retriever prompt and confirm its short list quickly.
beats.got: Four sessions, six prompts, and a thin file I'm told to push again. It's a lot of tab-juggling and it never says who in my team would do this or why.

beats.trigger: You can't yet tell if it is right; that is expected.
beats.got: The answer might be wrong and I'm told that's expected. That would worry me if I took it to the leadership team.

beats.trigger: Your team will ask: *when do I split, and how?*
beats.got: My team will want a rule for when to use several agents. Finally something I could be asked in a meeting.

beats.trigger: Build one agent per recurring workflow: a single `.md` file, guardrailed for that job.
beats.got: One agent per recurring workflow, like onboarding or the weekly people metrics. That maps to how HR already thinks about processes.

beats.trigger: If one agent can produce what you need, use one.
beats.got: Start simple and split only if you must. I like the restraint, and it's the opposite of hype.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.
beats.got: Different agents get different data access. That's the first time this module touched something my DPO would care about. I could ask the same question about employee data.

beats.trigger: Split for a reason, not because "three is more thorough"
beats.got: More agents isn't more careful. It's the same warning I'd give about adding more committees.

beats.trigger: The stances bring the variety. The frame brings the choice.
beats.got: You need a decision frame or you get a summary where nobody chose. That's true of my leadership meetings too.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output?
beats.got: A quick test of whether the split is real. I'd use it as a question for my team.

beats.trigger: **Helper agents in one session (the Phase 2 move).**
beats.got: Sessions versus helper agents. I lost the thread and 'Phase 2 move' refers to things I didn't register. Nothing in it mentions who does this work.

beats.trigger: Different tools: sessions; shared tools: helper agents.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a rule of thumb and I can't tell what I'd do with it.

beats.trigger: Splitting creates handoffs, and handoffs are where work goes wrong.
beats.got: Handoffs are where things break, with agents as with people. I know this from organisations, and it's the first slide that felt like my world.

beats.trigger: A whole module showed multi-agent works. Don't apply it to everything.
beats.got: A module on multi-agent that ends by telling you not to overuse it. That's credible, and it's the understatement I trust.

beats.trigger: Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.
beats.got: Agents fail in recognisable ways, and one is confident right before failing. That's a risk I could name.

beats.trigger: This prompt is long. Make your own variant.
beats.got: Nothing new. I'd have to do this with a long prompt I didn't write.

beats.trigger: move the risky step from "do" to "propose."
beats.got: When an agent is risky, change it from doing to proposing and add a human gate. That's a design principle I can use.

beats.trigger: rewrites the root instructions file in place and reports what changed.
beats.got: The agent rewrites a file of rules and reports back. I'm not sure what the root file is or who owns it.

beats.trigger: it does not check whether the briefing is true.
beats.got: The review checks how agents handed work over, not whether the result is true. Nobody here is checking it. I'd want that said to my leadership team.

beats.trigger: Read the agent's summary. Push back where it's wrong
beats.got: Push back on the agent's summary where it's wrong. That works only if I know enough to spot what's wrong.

beats.trigger: Keep the unease about the synthesized briefing as an open question. Do not fix it today.
beats.got: I'm told to leave my doubt about the answer unresolved. I'm uncomfortable carrying an unchecked result around.

beats.trigger: Memory is a working artefact, sharpened by what it bumps into.
beats.got: Nothing new. I'd skip it.

beats.trigger: Split only where agents can't be one: access, dialect, stance.
beats.got: Three reasons to split: access, dialect, stance. I can remember those.

beats.trigger: [Agent Trigger List, After Module 3]
beats.got: Two more links to supplementary reading.

beats.trigger: Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound.
beats.got: Agent risk sits on top of normal security, and I should write down what matters about my company's data. That is relevant for employee data.

beats.trigger: An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.
beats.got: Ask what an agent could do with its access. That's a question to bring to the DPO and works council before I do anything with people data.

beats.trigger: You're close to an agent system that cracks your crux.
beats.got: I'm told to keep building. I'm not close to cracking anything, and I still don't know who would own it.

take_homes: Start with one agent per recurring workflow and split only for a reason: different access, different dialect, different stance.
Handoffs between agents are where work goes wrong, and nothing in the exercises checks whether the synthesized answer is true.
Before I try any agent on people data, I need to ask what the worst thing is it could do with its access, and take that to the works council and the DPO.

monday.move: Email my DPO and one HR partner the question 'what could an agent do with access to our people-metrics data?' I won't build anything yet.
monday.who: Me, then the DPO and one HR business partner
monday.stop_condition: The DPO says which data is allowed in an AI tool. If they can't say, I stop there.
monday.blocker: Works council and DPO approval for employee data, which I haven't asked for yet. I also didn't get from this module who would own an agent after I leave.

misconception.why: The module never talked about roles or headcount. 'Hire three agents' and 'one agent per workflow' still sound to me like agents taking over work people do now, and I still don't know which roles.

one_line: The rule about when to split agents is sensible, but I did six prompts across four sessions and nobody said what it means for my people.
